# Convex-function mean sublevels and a shared endpoint-shadow center

This note supplies an exact whole-body shadow credit for a primitive
integer extrusion. The ordinary convex-function lemma holds in arbitrary
continuous dimension. Its application to the endpoint means below has
ONE integer coordinate. It is not a mixed-quotient Jensen theorem and
does not by itself prove a finite-extrusion OC bound.

Write Gamma_d=(d/(d+1))^d for d>=1.

## 1. A sharp mean-sublevel inequality for an actual convex function

Let K be a d-dimensional convex body, d>=1, and let f:K->R be bounded,
lower semicontinuous, and convex. With uniform probability on K, put
m=E f. Then

    |{x in K:f(x)<=m}| >= Gamma_d |K|.                           (1)

The analogous superlevel statement holds for a bounded upper
semicontinuous concave function. Closed level sets in (1) are essential
when the minimum has positive mass.

Here is a complete quantile proof. Normalize |K|=1 only in the notation,
and let F(t)=|{f<=t}|/|K|. The sublevel sets are compact convex. Convexity
of f gives

    (1-s){f<=t}+s{f<=u} subset {f<=(1-s)t+su}.

Brunn--Minkowski therefore makes F^(1/d) concave on its nonempty sublevel
domain. Define the root quantile

    q(r)=inf{t:F(t)>=r^d},       0<r<=1,
    q(0)=min_K f.

Every required quantile level is attained: compact sublevel sets decrease
to the limiting one, so their volumes are continuous from above. The
preceding sublevel inclusion and Brunn--Minkowski yield directly

    q((1-s)r+su)<=(1-s)q(r)+s q(u),       0<=r,u<=1.

For r=0 the nonempty minimum sublevel is retained, even if it has zero
volume. If it has positive mass, q is constant on the corresponding
initial r-interval; this is compatible with convexity. Thus no atom is
discarded and no strict inverse is presumed to exist.

For a uniform random variable U on [0,1], q(U^(1/d)) has distribution
function F. This follows directly from the defining quantile inequality,
or first at continuity levels and then by right continuity. Consequently

    E f=integral_0^1 q(r) d r^(d-1) dr
       >=q(integral_0^1 r d r^(d-1) dr)
       =q(d/(d+1)),

where the inequality is Jensen for the bounded convex q. Monotonicity of
F and the quantile property now give (1). If f is constant, (1) is
immediate and the same proof applies to its constant quantile.

The constant is sharp. On the standard d-simplex
K={x_i>=0, sum_i x_i<=1}, take f(x)=sum_i x_i. Then F(t)=t^d for
0<=t<=1, E f=d/(d+1), and equality holds in (1).

## 2. One deterministic interval of simultaneous shadow centers

Let C be a convex body in R_t times R^d_x, d>=1. Its ordinary projection
K onto the continuous coordinates is a d-dimensional convex body. Write
the actual nonempty vertical line sections as

    C_x=[a(x),b(x)],        x in K.

The function a is bounded lower semicontinuous and convex, while b is
bounded upper semicontinuous and concave. These assertions follow from
compactness and convexity of C. Let

    g=(1/|K|) integral_K x dx,
    a_bar=(1/|K|) integral_K a(x) dx,
    b_bar=(1/|K|) integral_K b(x) dx.

Every t_0 in [a_bar,b_bar] has both properties

    y=(t_0,g) in C,
    |projection_x(C intersect H)| >= Gamma_d |K|
       for EVERY closed ambient halfspace H containing y.      (2)

The first follows from ordinary Jensen:
a(g)<=a_bar<=t_0<=b_bar<=b(g).

For the second, first move a containing boundary parallel to itself
through y, only shrinking its intersection. Write this smaller cap as

    H={alpha(t-t_0)+u.(x-g)>=0},     (alpha,u)!=(0,0).

If alpha>0, a projected point is captured exactly when

    -b(x)-(u/alpha).(x-g)<=-t_0.

The left side is a convex function with mean -b_bar<=-t_0. Its sublevel
at the displayed threshold has at least the mass in (1). If alpha<0,
the projected condition is

    a(x)+(u/alpha).(x-g)<=t_0,

whose convex left side has mean a_bar<=t_0. Apply (1) again. If alpha=0,
the projection is K intersect {u.(x-g)>=0}; apply (1) to the affine
function -u.(x-g), of mean zero. This proves (2) for every oblique or
parallel direction with one fixed actual y. A tangential equality is
included by the closed inequalities.

## 3. Exact lattice membership, and its limitation

If [a_bar,b_bar] contains an integer j, then the point (j,g) in (2)
belongs to the original mixed-integer set. In particular,

    b_bar-a_bar=vol_(d+1)(C)/|K|>=1                              (3)

is a sufficient condition: choose j=ceil(a_bar). This is an actual
membership proof, not an untracked rounding of the ordinary centroid.

The interval need not contain an integer merely because C has nonempty
positive-volume integer fibers. For an exact planar example take

    0<=x<=1,        x/2-1/10<=t<=11/10-x/2.

Its quotient K is [0,1] and its mean endpoint interval is [3/20,17/20],
which misses the integers. Both actual integer fibers, at t=0 and t=1,
are the positive-length interval [0,1/5]. At g=1/2 there is no integer
point in the vertical line section of C. Thus the first assertion in (2)
must not be silently strengthened to mixed-integer membership without
the explicit integer-interval condition.

## 4. Payment in the WHOLE symmetric-extrusion cap

Assume such an integer j exists, put y=(j,g), A=|K|, and M=mu_MI(C).
For a nonnegative integer k let C_sym=C+[-k,k]e_t. The exact mass and
whole-cap inequalities proved in
`candidate 372cc3158e8582ae`
give

    mu_MI(C_sym)=M+2k A,
    mu_MI(C_sym intersect H)
       >=mu_MI(C intersect H)+k |projection_x(C intersect H)|.

Combining them with (2) proves, at the SAME original point y,

    D_(C_sym)(y)>=D_C(y)+k Gamma_d A.                            (4)

All D here are raw depths and all halfspaces are closed ambient
halfspaces. No separate favorable center is selected for the added
roof. The companion roof counterexample therefore does not contradict
(4): it concerns an isolated added law rather than this whole cap.

There is an exact limitation to the implication of (4). Subtracting the
desired n=1 raw OC target on C_sym from its proved right side gives

    [D_C(y)+k Gamma_d A]-(Gamma_d/2)[M+2k A]
       =D_C(y)-(Gamma_d/2)M.                                  (5)

Thus this estimate preserves the original point's target deficit; it
does not eliminate it by taking a finite or large k. If the source was
already deep enough, (4) proves that this particular extrusion preserves
its sharp normalized guarantee. If it was not, no such conclusion follows
from (4) alone. Formula (5) records the missing credit exactly.

## 5. Why the ordinary mean-sublevel step cannot use a mixed quotient

For integer N>=1 take the lattice triangle

    P=conv{(0,0),(N,0),(0,1)}.

Its integer points are (j,0), 0<=j<=N, and the apex (0,1). Under counting
measure, the affine (hence convex) function f(z)=-z_2 has mean
-1/(N+2). Only the apex satisfies f<=E f. Its fraction is 1/(N+2),
which tends to zero. Products with any positive-volume continuous convex
body give the same example for a mixed quotient.

Accordingly, Section 2 is specifically an n=1 application with ordinary
uniform quotient measure. The lattice quotient in a higher-integer-rank
primitive extrusion generally does not satisfy (1). A shared mixed
mean-sublevel theorem with constant Gamma_d is false, and is not used.

## 6. One primitive extrusion can require an entirely new mixed center

Here is an exact obstruction to retaining ANY original mixed center,
rather than merely a particular mean-endpoint choice. Put epsilon=1/100,
write x=(x_1,...,x_d), and take

    C={x in [0,1]^d,
          x_1/2-epsilon<=t<=1+epsilon-x_1/2}.

This is a full-dimensional convex polytope in R times R^d. Its integer
fibers occur only at t=0,1 and are both

    K_small=[0,2epsilon] times [0,1]^(d-1).

After the ONE symmetric primitive extrusion C^+=C+[-1,1]e_t, the only
integer fibers, in their order t=-1,0,1,2, are

    K_small,    K_full,    K_full,    K_small,
    K_full=[0,1]^d.

These assertions follow by substituting each integer t in the two
displayed affine endpoint inequalities. The total new mixed mass is
2+4epsilon=51/25, consistent with the exact extrusion identity.

Every point of the ORIGINAL mixed set has x_1<=2epsilon. The closed cap
{x_1<=2epsilon} contains all those possible old centers and has new mass

    2(2epsilon)+2(2epsilon)=8epsilon=2/25.

Consequently every original mixed point has new normalized depth at most
2/51. This is strictly below Gamma_d/2 in every d>=1: Gamma_d>1/3 gives
Gamma_d/2>1/6>2/51. The elementary bound Gamma_d>1/3 follows, for example,
from (1+1/d)^d<e<3.

The extruded body nevertheless has an explicit new point surpassing OC:

    y=(0,g),       g=(1/2,...,1/2).

It was not in the original mixed set. Its own full cube contributes at
least 1/2 to every containing halfspace, by central symmetry. For a cap
through y with nonzero continuous normal u, the traces on the two fibers
at t=-1 and t=1 have opposite thresholds relative to g. The reflection

    2g-K_small=[1-2epsilon,1] times [0,1]^(d-1)

is contained in the full cube at t=1. Reflection therefore shows that
these two traces together contribute at least |K_small|=2epsilon.
This is the partition of K_small into complementary closed continuous
halfspaces, whose common boundary has d-volume zero. For a purely
integer normal, the own fiber is included fully and at least one of
the paired fibers is included fully, giving an even stronger bound.
The final small fiber contributes nonnegative mass. Thus every closed
ambient halfspace containing y has raw mass at least

    1/2+2epsilon=13/25,

and y has normalized depth at least 13/51>1/4>=Gamma_d/2. The comparison
Gamma_d<=1/2 is valid for every d>=1, with equality at d=1.

For arbitrary n>=1, take the product of this construction with
[0,1]^(n-1) in additional integer coordinates. Each of its 2^(n-1)
binary-base copies is an actual copy of the preceding family. A finite
integer tilt isolates the old-source copy while retaining the cap
x_1<=2epsilon there, so every original mixed point has normalized depth
at most 2/[51*2^(n-1)], strictly below Gamma_d/2^n. Explicitly, subtract
2 times the affine Hamming-distance function from the cap margin
2epsilon-x_1; this excludes all other binary bases.

Conversely, the new point y in any binary copy gets raw mass at least
13/25 from that copy for every containing ambient halfspace. Dividing
by the full mass gives 13/[51*2^(n-1)]>Gamma_d/2^n. Hence an actual
new center succeeds in every n,d>=1, while EVERY old mixed point fails.

This is a center-relocation obstruction, not an OC counterexample. A
general extrusion argument must permit a new center and control its
whole cap; it cannot always propagate an original center's guarantee.
